questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the speed of a curve from its curvature
questions.stem: Another study group asks why the speed of a parameterised curve and its curvature are different quantities.

answer.exemplar: The speed is the length of the tangent vector, that is the magnitude of r'(t), and it says how fast the curve is being traced at a given moment. Curvature measures how sharply the tangent turns per unit length, so a curve can be traced quickly while bending gently, or slowly while turning sharply.

questions.explanation: Speed measures distance covered per unit time, while curvature measures how the direction of travel changes per unit of distance. They are independent, since a fast curve may bend very little.
questions.hint: Speed uses the tangent length, curvature uses its change.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: State the fundamental theorem of line integrals
questions.stem: A group reviewing the fundamental theorem of line integrals asks what it states about a potential function and a path.

answer.exemplar: If F is the gradient of a potential function f, then the line integral of F along any piecewise smooth path from A to B equals f(B) - f(A). The value therefore depends only on the two endpoints, so two different paths between the same points must give the same integral, and the path can be replaced by any other.

questions.explanation: The theorem turns a line integral into a difference of potential values at the endpoints. The hypothesis that the field is conservative is essential, and it is checked through a vanishing curl.
questions.hint: It gives endpoint values of the potential.

answer.exemplar: A definite integral is a signed accumulation, and reversing the limits means traversing the interval in the opposite direction, which cancels the contributions that were positive and flips those that were negative. answer.exemplar: Curvature is the rate at which the unit tangent changes direction per unit of arc length along the curve. questions.explanation: Curvature is measured per unit of distance travelled, so it compares how sharply the path bends rather than how fast the parameter runs. A straight line has zero curvature.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why exchanging limits changes the sign of a definite integral
questions.stem: A group asking why the value of a definite integral changes sign when the limits are exchanged listens for the reason.

answer.exemplar: A definite integral is a signed accumulation over the interval, and exchanging the limits means moving through the interval in the opposite direction. Every piece of the accumulation then contributes with the opposite sign, so the whole value is multiplied by minus one, and the antiderivative evaluation makes this visible.

questions.explanation: The definite integral is a signed accumulation. Evaluating the antiderivative at the limits in the written order makes this visible.
questions.hint: Reversing the direction of travel reverses the signs.

questions.learningObjective: Judge when a polar integral is preferable to a Cartesian one

answer.exemplar: Polar coordinates are preferable when the region is described by circles and radial directions, and when the integrand contains x squared plus y squared, since that becomes r squared and integrates much more simply. questions.explanation: Polar coordinates pay off when the region has circular boundaries or the integrand depends only on the distance from the origin. Straight-sided regions are usually better in Cartesian form.

answer.exemplar: When the integrand is one, the triple integral returns the volume of the solid, since each infinitesimal box contributes its own volume to the total. questions.explanation: The triple integral of one is the volume of the solid, because the integration simply sums the volumes of the small boxes. With a different integrand the sum is weighted.
